title: Regularity lifts from the quotient by a regular sequence
statement: Let $(R,\mathfrak m)$ be a commutative Noetherian local ring [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring], where local means having a unique maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$. Let $r\ge0$ and let $x_1,\ldots,x_r\in\mathfrak m$ be a regular sequence [def-weil-pbc-regular-sequence] in $R$. If the quotient ring $R/(x_1,\ldots,x_r)$ is regular local [def-weil-regular-scheme], then $R$ is regular local.

source.place: Tag 00NU, lemma-regular-mod-x, second assertion (including the empty sequence).

proof.text: Put $I_i=(x_1,\ldots,x_i)$, $R_i=R/I_i$, and $\mathfrak m_i=\mathfrak m/I_i$ for $0\le i\le r$. Each $I_i\subseteq\mathfrak m$ is proper. Each $R_i$ is Noetherian: if $J\subseteq R_i$ is an ideal, its inverse image in $R$ is finitely generated by [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring], and the images of those generators generate $J$. Each $R_i$ is local with unique maximal ideal $\mathfrak m_i$: a maximal ideal of $R_i$ has a field quotient, so its inverse image is maximal in $R$ and hence equals $\mathfrak m$; conversely $R_i/\mathfrak m_i=R/\mathfrak m$ is a field. In particular all these quotient rings are nonzero.

source.place: Tag 00NU, lemma-regular-mod-x, proof; expanded quotient checks and descending induction. Public tag page read 2026-10-16; local source archive missing.

proof.text: For $0\le i<r$, let $a_i$ be the image of $x_{i+1}$ in $R_i$. Then $a_i\in\mathfrak m_i$, and multiplication by $a_i$ on $R_i$ is injective by the defining condition of [def-weil-pbc-regular-sequence]. The surjection $q_i:R_i\to R_{i+1}$ has kernel $a_iR_i$: an element represented by $z\in R$ maps to zero exactly when $z\in I_i+(x_{i+1})$. Thus $R_i/a_iR_i$ is identified with $R_{i+1}$ by $(z+I_i)+a_iR_i\mapsto z+I_{i+1}$; the reverse map is given by the same representatives. These formulas prove well-definedness and that the maps are inverse ring homomorphisms, and identify the quotient maximal ideal with $\mathfrak m_{i+1}$.

source.place: Tag 00NU, lemma-regular-mod-x, proof; expanded quotient checks and descending induction. Public tag page read 2026-10-16; local source archive missing.

proof.text: For every $0\le i\le r$, apply [lem-weil-pbc-noetherian-local-finite-krull-dimension] to $R_i$ to write $d_i=\dim R_i\in\mathbf Z_{\ge0}$. For $i<r$, the Noetherian local ring $R_i$ and the nonzerodivisor $a_i\in\mathfrak m_i$ satisfy every hypothesis of [lem-weil-pbc-dimension-quotient-nonzerodivisor]. With the quotient identification in step 2 this gives $d_{i+1}+1=d_i$. Ring isomorphisms preserve Krull dimension here directly: image and inverse image send prime ideals to prime ideals and preserve strict inclusions, so give mutually inverse correspondences of chains of every length.

source.place: Tag 00KW, lemma-one-equation, nonzerodivisor equality; Tag 00KQ, proposition-dimension, finiteness for Noetherian local rings; used in Tag 00NU.

proof.text: Fix $i<r$ and suppose $R_{i+1}$ is regular local. By the regular-local-ring clause of [def-weil-regular-scheme], choose $d_{i+1}$ generators $\bar y_1,\ldots,\bar y_{d_{i+1}}$ of $\mathfrak m_{i+1}$, and choose lifts $y_j\in\mathfrak m_i$. Such lifts lie in $\mathfrak m_i$ because $q_i^{-1}(\mathfrak m_{i+1})=\mathfrak m_i$. For $z\in\mathfrak m_i$, write $q_i(z)=\sum_j\bar b_j\bar y_j$ and lift each coefficient $\bar b_j$ to $b_j\in R_i$. Then $z-\sum_jb_jy_j\in\ker q_i=a_iR_i$, so $z=c a_i+\sum_jb_jy_j$ for some $c\in R_i$. Conversely $a_i$ and all the $y_j$ belong to $\mathfrak m_i$. Hence $\mathfrak m_i=(a_i,y_1,\ldots,y_{d_{i+1}})$, a generating list of length $1+d_{i+1}=d_i$ by step 3. Since $R_i$ is Noetherian local by step 1, the same definition says $R_i$ is regular local. This argument also covers $d_{i+1}=0$, when the displayed sum is empty.

source.place: Tag 00NU, lemma-regular-mod-x, proof; expanded quotient checks and descending induction. Public tag page read 2026-10-16; local source archive missing.

proof.text: Use descending induction on $i$ with induction assertion that $R_i$ is regular local. The starting assertion $R_r=R/(x_1,\ldots,x_r)$ is the hypothesis. If the assertion holds for $i+1$, step 4 proves it for $i$. Therefore it holds for $i=0$, which is $R_0=R/(0)$ and identifies with $R$ by $z+(0)\mapsto z$. This identification sends maximal ideals and their generating lists to one another and preserves prime chains, so gives regularity of $R$ by the defining criterion. When $r=0$, the starting assertion is already the conclusion and no induction step or dimension-drop formula is used.
